abstract: |
  Value-added taxes (VAT) that credit purchases generate incentives for firms to overreport their inputs: every fictitious dollar of deductible inputs lowers their tax liability, and thus the higher the rate, the larger the incentive. However, how this evasion responds to the tax rate is largely unknown, because true inputs are not observed and firms that overreport may be mistaken for low-productivity firms. I separate overreporting from productivity using a structural production-function approach, with corporations, which government and market scrutiny keep from evading, as the truth-reporting benchmark. My method only requires input and output firm data and thus applies equally to standard firm-level surveys, administrative data, or confidential tax records. I apply it to Colombian manufacturing firms from 1981 to 1991, a period that includes a 1983 reform that raised the sales-tax rate for most industries. In Colombia, the sales tax worked as a VAT. Between 1983 and 1987, overreporting by unincorporated firms in the affected industries, measured as a share of true materials, rose by about 9 percentage points. I then estimate a structural model of tax evasion, including a detection probability and the cost of evasion, and find that a 0.5 percent increase in the sales-tax rate raises claimed deductions by between 16 and 28 percent, while cuts lower them only gradually: the smallest cut distinguishable from current policy is 8 percent. The approach also yields a statistical test for overreporting. Under the null hypothesis of no evasion, it is robust to a wide family of specifications of detection probabilities and costs of evasion. Its rejections can only point to overreporting. Among the 20 largest industries, the test detects overreporting in 9 of the 18 industries liable for the sales tax, including 4 of the 5 largest. Furthermore, the test does not detect evasion in either of the 2 largest exempt industries, as expected: these firms have no incentive to overreport. Among the 7 industries where the test rejects the absence of overreporting at the 1 percent level, firms overreport on average 16 percent of their true materials in the median industry. Finally, failing to correct for overreporting yields output elasticities of materials that are consistently larger, and productivity distributions that are more dispersed and less persistent: in the median industry, the 90–10 ratio is 66 percent larger and the half-life of productivity shocks is 52 percent shorter.
